summary: Defines an extension to the RSVP Explicit Route Object and Record Route Object that allows generic attributes to be specified or recorded for a particular hop of a label switched path. RFC 5420 handled attributes for the whole path.

eli5.summary: Travel directions with notes for each stop, not just the whole trip.

questions: what is the ero hop attributes subobject
how to signal per-hop attributes in mpls
subtitle: A way to attach attributes to one specific hop of an MPLS path instead of to the whole path.

tldr.problem: RFC 5420 lets RSVP-TE carry attributes that apply to a whole label switched path, but several other documents need attributes aimed at one particular hop along the path.
tldr.mechanism: A new Hop Attributes subobject, type 35, goes into the Explicit Route Object right after the subobject for the hop it describes, and carries a list of TLVs. A matching subobject in the Record Route Object lets nodes report back.
tldr.outcome: It is a generic building block: it does not say what the attributes mean, so other documents define the specific TLVs and flags that use it.

today: RFC 7570 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC names other documents, such as RFC 7571, as having identified a need for per-hop attributes.

sections.title: Why Per-Hop Attributes
sections.content:
In MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineering, a Label Switched Path (LSP) can be steered by an Explicit Route Object (ERO), a list of subobjects that name the nodes or links the path must pass through. RFC 5420 already lets RSVP-TE carry generic attributes, but they apply to the whole path.

Several other documents identified a need for attributes aimed at specific hops. This RFC gives them one generic mechanism instead of each inventing its own. It does not restrict what the information can be used for, and it builds on the LSP attributes of RFC 5420 so that they can be expressed in the ERO and in Secondary Explicit Route Objects (SEROs).
sections.eli5: Until now you could only attach one note to a whole journey. This document lets you attach a note to a single stop along the way.

sections.title: The ERO Hop Attributes Subobject
sections.content:
The ERO Hop Attributes subobject is OPTIONAL and is carried in the ERO or SERO. It uses the standard ERO subobject format. The L bit MUST be set to 0, and the Type is 35. After the Length comes a Reserved field that ends in the R bit, followed by a list of Hop Attributes TLVs.

Reserved MUST be set to 0 when the subobject is inserted, MUST NOT be changed when a node processes the ERO, and MUST be ignored on the node addressed by the preceding ERO subobjects.

The R bit reflects the LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTE versus LSP_ATTRIBUTE distinction from RFC 5420. When set, the hop attributes are required and must be processed by the node. When cleared, they are not required.

The size of the ERO subobject limits the Hop Attributes TLVs to 250 bytes. The RFC says the typical size of the currently defined and forthcoming TLVs is not foreseen to exceed this.
sections.eli5: It is a little tag stuck onto one stop on the route. A switch on the tag says 'you must follow this note' or 'follow it if you can'.

sections.title: Hop Attributes TLVs and Flags
sections.content:
The attributes are encoded as TLVs (type, length, value records) in the format from RFC 5420. A subobject may hold one or more TLVs, there are no ordering rules, and receivers SHOULD NOT read meaning into their order.

The Attribute Flags TLV from RFC 5420 can be carried here, and its flags are interpreted in the context of the received ERO. Only a subset of flags is valid in this place. Invalid flags SHALL be silently ignored, while unknown flags SHOULD trigger a PathErr with Error Code Unknown Attributes Bit.

Each document that defines a flag or TLV for this subobject has to say after which kinds of ERO subobject it is valid, whether ordering relative to other subobjects for the same hop (for example Label subobjects) matters, how it is interpreted if so, and what modification rules apply.
sections.eli5: The notes are short labeled items. Some labels are allowed on these stop-notes and some are not, and anyone who invents a new label has to explain where it can be used.

sections.title: How Nodes Process the ERO Subobject
sections.content:
One or more ERO Hop Attributes subobjects for a hop MAY be inserted directly after any of the existing identifying subobjects. If Label subobjects are present for that hop, the Hop Attributes subobject MAY also come after them. The attributes apply to the immediately preceding subobject or subobjects in the list.

When the R bit is set, a node MUST examine the TLVs following the rules in Section 5.2 of RFC 5420. When it is not set, the node MUST follow Section 4.2 of RFC 5420.

A node that does not understand the subobject behaves as RFC 3209 describes for an unrecognized ERO subobject: it returns a PathErr with Error Code Routing Error and Error Value Bad EXPLICIT_ROUTE object. The same error is used when a Hop Attributes TLV is longer than its subobject, and a node MUST NOT originate a TLV longer than the subobject.
sections.eli5: Each note belongs to the stop right before it. A switch that does not understand notes of this kind has to complain, in the way the older rules already say.

sections.title: Reporting Back with the RRO Hop Attributes Subobject
sections.content:
Sometimes it matters to know whether an optional hop attribute was actually processed. The RRO Hop Attributes subobject, also Type 35, is OPTIONAL and carried in the RECORD_ROUTE object. It has no L or R bit, only a Reserved field and the Hop Attributes TLVs, which hold the processed or additional attributes.

It MUST be pushed after the RRO Attributes subobject of RFC 5420 if one is present, and it MAY appear between subobjects identifying routers or links. Unless local policy applies, transit routers SHOULD forward these subobjects unmodified, although a node such as a domain edge node MAY prune or modify the RRO for confidentiality or to reduce its size.

The requirement to report compliance MUST be specified in the document that defines the use of the attribute. For attributes signaled in the LSP_ATTRIBUTES or LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES objects, a node SHOULD keep using the RRO Attributes subobject. For attributes signaled only in an ERO Hop Attributes subobject, a node SHOULD use the RRO Hop Attributes subobject and SHOULD NOT use the RRO Attributes subobject. An ingress that does not support it will drop the information.
sections.eli5: The way back works like a guest book. A stop can sign it to say 'I read your note', and the first station that does not know the guest book just ignores the signatures.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA allocated value 35 named Hop Attributes in the EXPLICIT_ROUTE registry (sub-object type 20) and the same value in the ROUTE_RECORD registry (sub-object type 21).

The Attribute Flags registry gained a new column headed ERO that says whether each flag may appear in the ERO Hop Attributes subobject. For all the flags that existed then (bits 0 to 12), the column is set to No, and new allocation requests SHALL state the value for it. The Attributes TLV Space registry gained a HOP_A column, where only the Attribute Flags TLV (type 1) is allowed on the hop subobject, while the Service ID TLV (type 2) and OAM Configuration TLV (type 3) are not.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers got one new entry, and two lists got a new column that says which items may be used in the new per-stop notes. At first only one kind may be.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no new security mechanisms and builds on RFC 3209 and RFC 5420. The existing RSVP considerations still apply.

The mechanism gives more control over LSP attributes at a given node. A node SHOULD check hop attributes against its policies and admission procedures like any other input, and MAY reject a message with errors such as Policy Control Failure or Admission Control Failure. Exposure of LSP requests to someone with unauthorized access can only be solved by encrypting the whole signaling message.

Reporting attributes in the RRO can reveal details about a node that an operator wants kept confidential. It is RECOMMENDED that domain boundary policies take the release of RRO hop attributes into consideration.
sections.eli5: A stop should treat the notes like any other request and may refuse them. Signing the guest book can tell outsiders things about the stop, so border guards should decide what to let through.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: Loose bit as in RFC 3209; MUST be set to 0.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: MUST be 0 on insert and is not changed by processing nodes.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: When set, the hop attributes are required.

cells: Ask for or require attributes at a hop
